Seedance 2.5: Native 30-second single-shot generation with whole-shot reasoning — identity, lighting and motion stay coherent far longer than rivals. Seven aspect ratios.
By far the priciest per second at 720p (~$0.47/s), and capped at 720p — no 1080p or 4K.
Seedance 2.0: Multi-shot editing, native audio, real-world physics and director-level camera control, with fast/mini tiers and reference-to-video across the line.
720p costs ~$0.30/s; 1080p more than doubles it. Prompt-following degrades on very long multi-shot scripts.
Kling 3: Native multi-shot (multi_prompt + shot_type) up to 15s with native audio — rare combination. Strong cinematic motion and camera language.
Audio-on roughly doubles cost. No resolution selector on the endpoint; 4K is a separate pricier endpoint.
MiniMax H3: Frontier MiniMax model — 2K and 4K output, 5–15s, seven aspect ratios, LoRA and reference modes.
Premium pricing at 2K/4K; 768p is the only cheap tier; ecosystem still young.
Veo 3.1: Best-in-class prompt adherence and native dialogue+SFX audio; 4K tier; reference-to-video and first/last-frame variants all share one quality bar.
Only 16:9 and 9:16, hard 8s ceiling, no multi-shot, and the most expensive per-second tier once audio is on. Heavy content filtering rejects many prompts.
FLUX.3 Video: BFL's frontier video model with a full control surface: t2v, i2v, first-last-frame and keyframes-to-video, each with a cheap draft mode.
Draft mode is 720p-only; the quality tier is expensive at 1080p ($0.29/s); very new, little community knowledge.
Kling 2.5T: Excellent motion fluidity and prompt precision at a low flat rate; the value pick in the Kling line.
No audio at all, 5s/10s only, 1:1/16:9/9:16 only.
Grok Imagine: Very cheap audio-included generation ($0.07/s at 720p); fast turnaround.
Lower fidelity than 1.5, limited duration and aspect control.
Gemini Omni Flash: Synchronized audio plus Gemini's real-world grounding and physics understanding — the best 'plausible world' model.
Google safety filtering is aggressive; limited duration and aspect control; reference mode is basic.
Kling 2.6: Cheapest Kling tier with native audio ($0.07/s audio-off). Good quality-per-dollar for social content.
No multi-shot, no explicit resolution control, and audio doubles the price.
Kling Lipsync: Cheap ($0.014/input-second) re-dubbing of an existing video with accurate mouth shapes.
Edits an existing clip only — it generates nothing. Billing rounds up to 5s increments.
Seedance 1.5: Very good quality-per-dollar with audio (~$0.26 for a 720p 5s clip); solid all-rounder.
Token-based pricing is hard to predict; fewer control knobs than 2.x; no multi-shot.
Kling 1.6: Cheap workhorse with an 'elements' mode for multi-subject composition; still fine for simple motion.
Dated visual quality, visible artifacting on fast motion, no audio.
Seedance 1.0: Fast tier is genuinely cheap for 1080p; clean, stable motion for product and b-roll shots.
No audio, no reference mode, and superseded by 1.5/2.x on realism.
Wan 2.7: Latest Wan: smoother motion, better scene fidelity and coherence, with a reference-to-video mode.
New enough that community LoRA/tooling support lags 2.2; pricing sits above the 2.2 tiers.
Kling O3: Kling's realism-tuned line: strong physical plausibility, plus reference-to-video and 4K variants. Cheaper than v3 at the standard tier.
Fewer creative/stylized results than v3; audio surcharge; reference fidelity trails Vidu/Seedance on multi-subject scenes.
Pixverse V6: Newest Pixverse: best prompt adherence in the line, with transition mode included.
Sparse documentation; audio support unclear; Pixverse's stylized bias persists.
Wan 2.5/2.6: Strong all-round open-weight quality with audio support; the 2.6 flash tier is fast and cheap.
Preview-grade stability; documentation and parameter surface keep shifting between versions.
Hailuo 02: Best-in-class physical motion (the 'gymnast' benchmark model); very cheap standard tier at $0.045/s.
768p standard / 1080p pro only, no aspect control, no audio, fixed durations.
LTX-2.3: Widest configuration surface on fal — 22B/quality/distilled/LoRA variants, audio, and per-megapixel billing that makes short clips very cheap.
Endpoint sprawl is confusing; the base 2.3 tier starts at 1080p (no cheaper 720p tier); LoRA variants cost more per megapixel.
Wan 2.2 A14B: The open-weights sweet spot — LoRA support, turbo tier, 480p/580p/720p control, huge community ecosystem.
No native audio, 81–161 frame ceiling (~5–10s at 16fps), and 16fps output needs interpolation for smooth playback.
Grok Imagine 1.5: Audio included at every tier, three resolutions with transparent per-second pricing, and reference-to-video support.
xAI content policy is idiosyncratic; 1080p only on t2v; quality trails Veo/Kling on complex scenes.
Alibaba Happy Horse: 1080p with synchronized native audio, 3–15s, five aspect ratios, and a reference-to-video mode — a very complete feature set.
Little independent evaluation available; v1.1 and v1.0 differences are undocumented.
LTX-Video (legacy): Extremely fast and cheap; fully open weights; good for previews and iteration.
Visibly dated quality — soft textures, weak coherence past ~3s, no audio.
LTX-2.5: Open-source synchronized audio+video in one pass; pro/fast tiers; best open alternative to Veo for talking scenes.
Newer and less battle-tested; megapixel billing punishes long or high-res renders.
Kling 2.1: Master tier still has the most cinematic look of the older Kling generations; three price tiers (std/pro/master) for the same API shape.
Master is expensive ($1.40/5s), no audio, and superseded by 2.5T/3 on both price and quality.
Kling 2.0: Master-grade visuals with simple, stable API; good for period/cinematic looks.
Legacy — no audio, no multi-shot, priced above newer and better tiers.
Hailuo 2.3: Outstanding motion realism and character physics for the price; standard tier is one of the best value picks on fal.
Fixed 6s/10s durations, no aspect-ratio control on most endpoints, no native audio.
Kling 1.0: Lowest-cost entry into the Kling API surface; effects presets included.
Clearly obsolete quality — soft detail, weak prompt adherence, no audio.
Pika 2.2: Pikaframes (2–5 keyframes with per-transition prompts) enables ~25s multi-beat sequences; Pikascenes composes multiple subjects.
1080p costs 2.25x 720p; no audio; character consistency drifts across keyframes.
Wan 2.1: Battle-tested open model with t2v/i2v/flf2v/effects endpoints and LoRA support; very cheap.
Wan 2.2 5B: Cheapest credible 720p generation on the platform (~$0.30/min via distill/fast-wan tiers); runs almost anywhere.
5B capacity shows on complex motion and faces; 5s cap; no audio.
Luma Ray 3.2: Cinematic look with seamless looping control and reference images to lock subject/style — the loop feature is nearly unique.
Premium pricing; smaller ecosystem; no native audio.
Pixverse V5: Very cheap ($2.40/min at 720p), five aspect ratios, effects and transition endpoints.
No audio, 5s/8s only, and a persistent over-saturated 'AI video' look.
MiniMax video-01: Director endpoint exposes explicit camera-movement commands; 'live' variant is tuned for illustration/anime motion.
Fixed 6s at 720p, no audio, and quality is a generation behind Hailuo 02/2.3.
Mirage Avatar-X: Industry-leading identity preservation and expressivity, with up to 180s of speech — the longest avatar output here.
Voice reference constraints (10–180s) add setup friction; premium positioning.
Vidu Q3: Strong multi-reference consistency (mix mode) and 1–16s continuous duration control across four resolutions.
The 2.2x multiplier for 720p/1080p makes it pricey (~$9.24/min); audio support is thin.
Hunyuan (legacy): Open weights with excellent text-video alignment for its generation; strong motion diversity.
129-frame cap, no audio, slow, and superseded by Hunyuan 1.5.
Pixverse C1: Film-grade tier with native audio, up to 1080p and 15s, plus reference-to-video — the strongest Pixverse offering.
Priced well above the numbered Pixverse tiers; newer and less documented.
Luma Ray 2: Genuinely natural, coherent camera motion — still one of the most 'filmed' looking models. Flash tier is cheap.
No audio, fixed 5s, and detail resolution trails newer models.
HeyGen: Production-grade digital twins with lip-sync, backgrounds, captions and MP4/WebM output; avatar3/4/5 tiers plus video-agent endpoints.
Requires avatar setup; costly at $0.10/s for avatar4; presenter-framing only.
Pixverse V4.5: Broad endpoint family (t2v/i2v/effects/transition/fast) at low cost; good template effects library.
Superseded by V5+; no audio; motion artifacts on complex scenes.
LTX-2 19B: Cheap per-megapixel pricing, native audio, LoRA support and up to 481 frames — the best cost-per-frame in the quality tier.
Megapixel billing means cost scales with resolution AND length; motion is less cinematic than Kling/Veo.
Pixverse V5.5: Adds multi-clip mode and audio while staying at $0.20 per 5s 720p clip — excellent value.
Multi-clip and audio both add surcharges that the headline price hides.
Hunyuan 1.5: Tencent's best open model — strong motion and detail at $0.045/s, with an image-to-video variant.
Only one resolution tier documented; no audio; smaller LoRA ecosystem than Wan.
CogVideoX: Fully open 5B weights, easy to self-host, decent prompt following for its size.
Kling 1.5: Pro-tier effects endpoints and dependable image-to-video for simple shots.
Superseded on every axis; no audio, low resolution ceiling.
VEED: Fabric 1.0 turns a single photo into a talking presenter at $0.35/minute — the cheapest talking-head on the platform.
Head-and-shoulders framing only; limited expressiveness; no scene generation.
Vidu Q2: Best-in-class subject reference fidelity for the money; pro and turbo tiers.
Odd hybrid pricing (per-request + per-second) is hard to forecast; 720p tier is limited.
Ovi: Unified audio+video generation in one pass at $0.20 per 5s clip — cheap synchronized sound.
Fixed 5s and low resolution; audio quality is rough compared to Veo/LTX-2.5.
Pixverse V5.6: Higher-fidelity tier with audio and transition support.
Noticeably pricier than V5.5 ($0.45 vs $0.20 per 5s at 720p) for a modest jump.
Vidu Q1: Reliable 1080p at a flat $0.40 per 5s clip, with reference and start-end modes.
Fixed 5s, no audio, and motion is stiffer than Kling/Hailuo.
fal AI-Avatar: Infinitalk and the multi-speaker endpoints handle two-person conversations — rare among avatar models.
$0.20/s for the multi endpoint is steep; faces drift on long takes.
Kandinsky 5: Flat $0.05–$0.16 per clip regardless of resolution — extremely predictable cost. Distill tier is very fast.
Lower fidelity than Wan/LTX at the same price; no audio; 5s/10s only.
T2V-Turbo: Fast and cheap short clips for prototyping.
Cosmos Predict 2.5: Physically grounded world simulation from NVIDIA; deterministic fixed output makes it reproducible.
Fixed 1280x704 and 93 frames — no duration, resolution or aspect control at all; no audio.
Pixverse V4: Cheap and fast with the full effects/transition surface.
Dated quality, no audio, weak text rendering.
LongCat: Purpose-built for long-form: 720p/30fps with a distilled tier at $0.01 per generated second — the cheapest long video on fal.
Quality is clearly below frontier models; separate endpoints per resolution; no audio.
Wan Pro: Premium 1080p at 30fps with excellent motion diversity for a Wan 2.1-era model.
1080p-only (no cheap 720p tier), fixed 6s, expensive relative to Wan 2.2, no audio.
Kandinsky 5 Pro: Fast high-quality diffusion with a 1024p tier; genuinely open Russian-lab alternative.
No 720p tier (512p or 1024p only), so 720p work overpays; no audio; weak English prompt nuance.
SVD: Historically important, extremely cheap, and fast; good for subtle image animation.
25 frames at 6–10fps, no prompt control in the classic sense, no audio — effectively a motion-nudge tool.
AnimateDiff: Cheap stylized/anime motion with a turbo tier; strong LoRA compatibility.
Very short, low resolution, flickery — a 2023-era pipeline.
Bernini-R: ByteDance's unified generation + editing model — one endpoint for both, with reference support.
Editing-oriented; documentation is minimal; not tuned for pure cinematic output.
Krea-Wan: Krea's aesthetic tuning on Wan 14B gives a distinctly more stylish, less 'AI-looking' image for $0.025/s.
Single t2v endpoint only; 16fps; no audio or image conditioning.
MAGI: Exceptional understanding of physical interaction and cinematic prompts for a distilled model.
$0.32 per 4s is poor value now; 96-frame cap; inference-step surcharges stack quickly.
Moonvalley Marey: Trained exclusively on fully licensed data — the only clearly clean-rights model on the platform, which matters for commercial work.
By far the most expensive ($1.50 per 5s = $18/min); no audio; slower than everything else.
Infinity-Star: 8B spacetime autoregressive engine — roughly 10x faster than diffusion at 720p, for $0.07 per video.
Very short clips, minimal control surface, and quality well below diffusion peers.
Pixverse V3.5: Lowest-cost Pixverse tier; fine for simple looping social clips.
Clearly obsolete; soft detail and unstable faces.
Pika 2.1: Strong character control and cinematic camera moves for the price.
Pika 2 Turbo: Fastest Pika tier — good for rapid iteration.
Lowest quality in the Pika line; 5s; no audio.
Argil: Avatar videos generated straight from text with a natural, non-uncanny feel.
Closed avatar library; little control over framing or scene.
Kling Avatar: Audio-driven talking avatars up to 60s that handle humans, animals, cartoons and stylized characters equally well.
Pro tier costs 2x Standard for modest gains; body motion below the neck is limited; needs a clean single-speaker audio track.
OmniHuman: Emotion and body motion correlate strongly with the audio, not just lips — the most lifelike audio-driven human model.
Needs a good full-figure reference image; ~30s ceiling; no scene control.
Kling O1: Purpose-built start-frame → end-frame interpolation with text-guided styling; very reliable transitions.
Narrow use case — it is an in-betweener, not a general generator. No audio.
Talking-head (legacy): Nearly free (GPU-second billed) and instant; SadTalker/MuseTalk/LivePortrait are fine for quick previews.
Obvious artifacts, small motion range, and dated quality — not client-ready.
Sync Lipsync: Works on illustrations and animated frames, not just photoreal faces.
Pixverse misc: Swap replaces people, objects or backgrounds inside an existing clip — a genuinely rare capability.
Editing tool, not a generator; quality depends heavily on the input video.
Utility: Deterministic and nearly free — exactly what you want for stitching or interpolation.
Not generative at all; no creative control.
Vidu 1.x: Cheapest reference-to-video and start-end-to-video on the platform; template mode gives one-click trends.
4s fixed, low resolution, visibly dated motion.
FramePack: Autoregressive generation keeps memory flat, so it handles longer clips cheaply; flf2v variant supports end frames.
Slow, 30fps-but-soft output, and drift accumulates over long generations.
Cosmos 3: NVIDIA omnimodal world model — video, audio and action commands from text/image/video/trajectory inputs. Unique for robotics and simulation.
Aimed at world-modeling, not aesthetics; sparse documentation; niche.
ByteDance Lynx: Very strong subject consistency from a single reference image.
Single endpoint, minimal controls, short output.
Decart Lucy: Real-time class: 5-second i2v in under 5 seconds (>1x realtime) — the fastest i2v on fal.
Quality is traded for speed; 5s fixed; no audio or fine control.
